### 1. Housing Trust Fund / Affordable Housing Fund
**Official program name:** Affordable Housing Trust Fund.[1]  
**Administering city department:** Community Development Department (staff administers per City Council Resolution 14760).[1]  
**Fund sources:** In-lieu fees, general fund allocations, and other contributions (e.g., City Council approved $600,000 allocation to nonprofits from the fund, exceeding initial $500,000 NOFA by $100,000).[1][3]  
**Annual funding available:** Capped at $250,000 per year through rolling applications unless City Council authorizes more; recent NOFA advertised up to $500,000, increased to $600,000.[1][3]  
**Eligible activities:** Supports affordable housing developers for projects serving lower/moderate-income households, seniors, people with disabilities, and formerly homeless individuals (e.g., grants for apartment acquisition, rehabilitation, planning/entitlements like $250,000 to Marin Foster Care Association, $200,000 to Abode, $150,000 to EAH Housing).[1][3]  
**Application process and cycles:** Rolling applications; periodic Notices of Funding Availability (NOFA). Current joint NOFA with Marin County (issued Jan 22, 2025) open through Feb 19, 2025, at 5 PM for over $3.6M including city funds.[1]  
**Affordability period requirements:** At least 55 years of income and rent restrictions for supported units.[1]  
**Contact information:** Community Development Department; for CDBG/HOME details, Marin County Federal Grants at (415) 499-6695.[1]  
**Official city website URL:** https://www.cityofsanrafael.org/funding-for-housing-projects/[1]  

**Resident input opportunities:** Public testimony at City Council meetings influences allocations (e.g., testimony led to full $250,000 grant for foster youth housing); NOFAs allow applications with council review.[1][3]  
**How residents can leverage at city council meetings:** Submit public comments during NOFA award hearings to advocate for specific projects or increases (e.g., foster advocates swayed council to boost funding).[3]  
**Key leverage points for civic engagement:** Attend council sessions for NOFA approvals; join public input on fund guidelines per Resolution 14760.[1][3]

### 2. Inclusionary Housing Requirements
No specific details on inclusionary housing requirements, such as unit percentages, project thresholds, in-lieu fees, adjustment methodology, compliance options, or governing ordinances, were found in city sources. Limited mentions of related commitments exist, like the city's agreement to zone/permit at least 80 permanent affordable units (for households <80% AMI) at 350 Merrydale Road by June 30, 2028, or face county penalties.[2] Residents can engage via public hearings on zoning changes tied to such projects.[2]

### 3. Commercial Linkage Fees
No information found on commercial linkage fees, including rates by building type, thresholds, nexus studies, or usage.

### 4. Local Ballot Measures (housing-related)
No details on recent (2020-2024) housing-related ballot measures, such as parcel taxes, funding, rates, revenue, or exemptions, were identified in sources.

### 5. Federal/State Pass-Through Programs
**City's share of CDBG funding:** Approximately $1.5M available via joint Marin County NOFA (2025-26 cycle open through Feb 19, 2025).[1]  
**HOME program participation:** Approximately $700K via same joint NOFA; city participates through cooperative agreement with Marin County Federal Grants division for San Rafael Planning Area allocations.[1]  
**Any cooperative agreements with county:** Yes, with Marin County for CDBG/HOME; also multi-jurisdictional for Merrydale Road projects (county provides $8M from its Affordable Housing Trust).[1][2]  
**How residents can influence local allocation priorities:** Through county NOFA process; contact Marin County Federal Grants at (415) 499-6695.[1]  

**Resident input opportunities:** Public comment periods during county NOFA cycles and city council reviews of pass-through uses.[1]  
**How residents can leverage at city council meetings:** Advocate during approvals of county agreements or project uses (e.g., Merrydale interim housing).[1][2]  
**Key leverage points for civic engagement:** Participate in joint NOFA applications and city council resolutions on housing crisis declarations streamlining permits.[1][2]

### 6. Other Municipal Housing Programs
**Below Market Rate (BMR) rental programs:** No dedicated BMR program details; related support via Trust Fund for deed-restricted rentals (e.g., 6 apartments for foster youth, 28-unit rehab at 455 Canal St.).[3] Highlands of Marin offers low/moderate-income units in partnership with city.[7]  
**Homeownership assistance programs:** None identified.  
**Tenant protection programs:** None specified.  
**Anti-displacement strategies:** Interim shelter at 350 Merrydale Road (65 tiny homes for up to 70 unhoused, with services, closing by 2029 unless extended; $12.5M total, city declares housing crisis for CEQA exemption/permit streamlining).[2][5]  

**Resident input opportunities:** Public meetings (e.g., Oct 28, Nov 6, Dec 9, Jan 14 for Merrydale program design/site policies); council hearings (e.g., 3 hours of comments before Merrydale approval).[2]  
**How residents can leverage at city council meetings:** Provide testimony on project approvals (e.g., neighborhood backlash noted but project advanced).[2]  
**Key leverage points for civic engagement:** Attend site-specific public sessions; comment on housing crisis declarations enabling streamlined affordable projects.[2]

PROGRAM: Below Market Rate Rental Program
program_name: Below Market Rate Rental Program
administering_agency: NOT_FOUND
description: The City of San Rafael maintains below market rate (BMR) rental units throughout the city, with each property managing its own application process and eligibility criteria based on income, household size, senior status, and other factors. Residents must contact individual properties to confirm availability, open waitlists, and submit applications directly to property managers. Examples include properties like Martinelli House (seniors 62+ at or below 50% AMI), Centertown, Riviera Apartments, Sundance Apartments, Turina House, and Highlands of Marin (with specific income limits up to moderate-income levels).[1][3][4][5][6]
income_limits: Varies by property (e.g., 50% AMI for Martinelli House seniors; up to $179,300 for 5-person households at Highlands of Marin)
official_url: https://www.cityofsanrafael.org/affordable_housing/[3]

**PROGRAM: Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) Program**  
administering_agency: Marin Housing Authority  
description: Provides rental assistance to very low-income individuals and families in Marin County to afford decent, safe housing in the private market. Applications are managed through the Marin Housing Authority's Rent Café portal for waitlists. Contact Marin Housing Authority for waitlist and application details.[1][7]  
official_url: https://www.marinhousing.org/find-housing[7]  

**PROGRAM: Public Housing Program**  
administering_agency: Marin Housing Authority (for County of Marin)  
description: Offers affordable rental housing units to eligible low-income families at affordable rates. Applications available via Rent Café Resident Portal for waitlists.[7]  
official_url: https://www.marinhousing.org/find-housing[7]
